## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sakulātherīgāthā* (Thig 5.7) is a short poetic text preserved in the fifth chapter (the *Pañcakanipāta*) of the *Therīgāthā* in the Pali Canon [SuttaCentral]. The poem records the spiritual attainments of the elder nun Sakulā (or Sākulā), who went forth after hearing the Dhamma from a monk and abandoning her home life, including her son, daughter, money, and grain [Sujato 2009; Swearer 2010]. In her stanzas, she describes cultivating the spiritual path and abandoning greed, hatred, and defilements while still training as a probationer (*sikkhamānā*), subsequently realizing full liberation and arahantship [Sujato 2009]. Sakulā is widely known across early Buddhist literature as the nun declared foremost among those possessing the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) [Harvey 2000; Edelglass and Garfield 2009; Collett 2014]. In modern scholarship, her verses have been closely examined in discussions of the *bhikkhunī* Vinaya to understand the evolution of the *sikkhamānā* training and the admission of married or mature women (*gihigatā*) into the order [Sujato 2009].

SuttaCentral records thirteen translations across ten languages, including modern English translations by Ayya Soma and Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral]. Although SuttaCentral lists no direct canonical parallels in other collections [SuttaCentral], Sakulā's status as foremost in the divine eye is recognized in parallel lists across traditions, such as the Pali *Aṅguttara Nikāya* and the Chinese *Ekottarika Āgama* [Collett 2014; Anālayo 2017]. The verses are cited and explained in the *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, with DharmaNexus recording five matching segments across verses 0.3–6.1 [DharmaNexus; Sujato 2009]. DharmaNexus also aligns several verse segments automatically with the Tibetan *Karmaśataka* (D0340) [DharmaNexus].
